transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi. Well, I guess I'm here because the regular clinic doctor got on me about my eating. I don't really see the issue, but most days I just keep it simple. I'll have coffee in the morning, maybe a few bites of something between painting jobs, and a small dinner if I'm not too busy catching up on my class paperwork.
Have you noticed any changes in your weight over the past few months, or has anyone commented on your weight?

I mean, yeah, I guess I've noticed a little. My work pants hang pretty loose on me now. And people on the job sites, they keep saying I look too thin. But... I don't really see it that way. I see it more like I've just leaned out from staying on my feet all day working.
When you're eating less, is that something you're actively trying to do, or does it just happen because you're busy with work and school?

I think it's mostly just... being busy, honestly. Between the painting jobs and my classes, I just don't really have the time to sit down and think about food. I guess I don't go out of my way to eat a lot, but I wouldn't say I'm actively trying to do it on purpose. It just sort of happens with my schedule.
When you look in the mirror, how do you feel about your body and your weight right now?

Honestly, when I look in the mirror, I just see myself. I don't really think my weight is some kind of emergency, like everyone else keeps acting. I mean, to me, it just feels like they're making a huge deal out of me being disciplined and busy with my life. I think I look fine.
Do you ever do anything to try to control your weight or compensate for what you eat—like exercising a lot, using laxatives, or making yourself vomit?

No, I don't do any of that stuff. I don't use laxatives or make myself throw up, and I don't really have time to work out on top of everything else. Like I said, I'm just busy. I'm on my feet painting all day, so I guess that's a lot of physical activity, but I'm not doing it to lose weight. It's just my job.
If you had more free time and weren't so busy with work and school, do you think you would eat more food, or would you still prefer to eat small amounts?

I'm not really sure. I haven't had a lot of free time lately to even find out. I guess... I'd probably just eat the way I do now. My body is pretty used to it at this point, so I don't know if having a few extra hours in the day would make me suddenly want to eat a lot more. I just eat what I need and get on with things, you know?
If you were to gain weight or eat more food, how would that make you feel emotionally? Would you be worried or upset about it, or would it just be a neutral change to you?

I wouldn't say it's neutral. Actually, if I eat something heavy... like a big sandwich or pizza, I get this panicky feeling. I just start worrying that I'll wake up bigger and slower. I'm up and down ladders all day for work, moving around different rooms, and I need to be able to move the way I always do. So yeah, the idea of eating more or gaining weight definitely makes me worried.
When did you first start eating noticeably less than you used to? Was there a specific time when you made a conscious decision to cut back, or has it always been this way for you?

I'm not really sure, honestly. It wasn't like I woke up one day and made a conscious decision to just... stop eating as much. I think it just happened gradually. I haven't always been this way, but I really couldn't give you a specific time or year when it started. It just sort of became my normal over time, I guess.
When you look at your body, do you ever feel like you look fat or overweight, or do you see yourself as thin?

I don't really know how to answer that. I guess I don't really see myself as either one. I just... I look in the mirror and I just see myself. I don't really focus on whether I look fat or thin. I'm just focused on making sure I can still do my job and get through the day. So, I don't really have a strong feeling about it either way.
When you imagine yourself at a heavier weight—say 20 pounds heavier than you are now—how would you feel about that? Would it bother you a lot, or would it not really matter to you?

I'm not really sure how to picture 20 pounds, to be honest. I haven't really thought about a specific number like that. I just know what I said earlier—that getting heavier would bother me because it would make moving around for my work a lot harder. But as for imagining that exact amount of weight... I don't really know. I just don't really think about it in those terms.

You mentioned earlier that people at work say you look too thin, and your pants are loose. Given that others are noticing you're thin, do you actually believe they're right about that, or do you think they're wrong and you're not actually thin?

I mean, I hear what they're saying, but I don't really think my weight is some emergency like everyone keeps acting. I guess I am thin, but to me, it just feels like they're making a big deal out of me being disciplined and busy with work. I don't think it's as serious as they make it out to be.

You mentioned that eating something heavy makes you panicky and worried about waking up bigger and slower. When you feel that worry about gaining weight or getting bigger, is that fear something that's really important to you and that you think about a lot? Or is it more of a practical concern just about your job performance?

I mean, it's mostly about the job, but... yeah, I guess the feeling itself is pretty strong. Like, if I were to eat something really heavy, like a big slice of pizza or a huge sandwich, I get this... this panicky feeling. It's hard to explain, but I just get really worried that I'll wake up the next day and be bigger, and slower. And if that happens, I won't be able to climb up and down the ladders or move around the rooms the way I need to for work. So I guess the fear is there, and I do think about it when I'm faced with that kind of food.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for Anorexia Nervosa (F50.0). Despite attributing reduced intake to busyness, there is clear evidence of: (1) significantly restricted energy intake leading to low body weight (loose work pants, observable weight loss, others noting 'too thin'), (2) intense fear of weight gain triggered by eating ('panicky feeling' about gaining weight and becoming 'bigger and slower'), and (3) disturbance in body image perception (minimizing concern about being thin, not viewing weight loss as problematic despite external evidence). The absence of compensatory behaviors (purging, laxatives, excessive exercise) and relatively preserved insight into being 'thin' suggest the restrictive subtype.
